"Kansas City" is a rhythm and blues song written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller in 1952. First recorded by Little Willie Littlefield the same year, as "K. C. Loving", the song later became a chart-topping hit when it was recorded by Wilbert Harrison in 1959. "Kansas City" is one of Leiber and Stoller's "most recorded tunes, with more than three hundred versions", with several appearing in the R&B and pop record charts.

sections.heading: Original song
sections.wikitext:
"Kansas City" was written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, two nineteen-year-old rhythm and blues fans from [[Los Angeles]].  Neither had been to [[Kansas City, Missouri|Kansas City]], but were inspired by [[Big Joe Turner]] records.<ref name="Marsh"/> 
{{poemquote|I'm goin' to Kansas City, Kansas City here I come (2×)
They got a crazy way of lovin' there, and I'm gonna get me some
I'm gonna be standing on the corner, of Twelfth Street and Vine (2×)
With my Kansas City baby, and a bottle of Kansas City wine}}
Through a connection to producer [[Ralph Bass]], they wrote "Kansas City" specifically for [[West Coast blues]]/R&B artist [[Little Willie Littlefield]].<ref name="Leiber">
{{Cite book
| last1 = Leiber
| first1 = Jerry
| author-link1 = Jerry Leiber
| last2 = Stoller
| first2 = Mike
| author-link2 = Mike Stoller
| last3 = Ritz
| first3 = David
| author-link3 = David Ritz
| title = Hound Dog: The Leiber and Stoller Autobiography
| publisher = [[Simon & Schuster]]
| year = 2009
| isbn = 978-1-4165-5938-2
| page = [https://archive.org/details/hounddogleiberan00leib/page/59 59]
| url = https://archive.org/details/hounddogleiberan00leib/page/59
}}</ref> There was an initial disagreement between the two writers over the song's melody: Leiber (who wrote the lyrics) preferred a traditional blues song, while Stoller wanted a more distinctive vocal line; Stoller ultimately prevailed. They taught the song to Littlefield at [[Maxwell Davis]]' house, who arranged and provided the tenor sax for the song.<ref name="Leiber"/> Littlefield recorded the song in Los Angeles in 1952, during his first recording session for [[Federal Records]], a [[King Records (United States)|King Records]] subsidiary. Federal's Ralph Bass changed the title to "K. C. Loving",<ref name=pc13>{{Pop Chronicles |13| 4|Leiber & Stoller}}</ref> which he reportedly considered to sound "hipper" than "Kansas City". Littlefield's record had some success in parts of the U.S., but it did not reach the national chart.

"Kansas City" was written by Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, two nineteen-year-old rhythm and blues fans from Los Angeles.  Neither had been to Kansas City, but were inspired by Big Joe Turner records. 
{{poemquote|I'm goin' to Kansas City, Kansas City here I come (2×)
They got a crazy way of lovin' there, and I'm gonna get me some
I'm gonna be standing on the corner, of Twelfth Street and Vine (2×)
With my Kansas City baby, and a bottle of Kansas City wine}}
Through a connection to producer Ralph Bass, they wrote "Kansas City" specifically for West Coast blues/R&B artist Little Willie Littlefield. There was an initial disagreement between the two writers over the song's melody: Leiber (who wrote the lyrics) preferred a traditional blues song, while Stoller wanted a more distinctive vocal line; Stoller ultimately prevailed. They taught the song to Littlefield at Maxwell Davis' house, who arranged and provided the tenor sax for the song. Littlefield recorded the song in Los Angeles in 1952, during his first recording session for Federal Records, a King Records subsidiary. Federal's Ralph Bass changed the title to "K. C. Loving", which he reportedly considered to sound "hipper" than "Kansas City". Littlefield's record had some success in parts of the U.S., but it did not reach the national chart.

sections.heading: Little Richard versions
sections.wikitext:
In 1955, [[Little Richard]] recorded two rather different versions of "Kansas City", both of which were not released until years later.<ref name="Ace">
{{cite AV media notes
| year = 1989
| title = Little Richard{{snd}}The Specialty Sessions
| type = Box set booklet
| others = [[Little Richard]]
| location = London
| publisher = [[Ace Records (United Kingdom)|Ace Records]]
| id = ABOXLP 1 (set), ABOXBK1 (booklet)
| page = 29
}}</ref> The first version, which was close to the original song, was released in November 1970, on the compilation album ''Well Alright!''.  Little Richard substantially re-worked the song for his second version, particularly the refrain starting with words "Hey, hey, hey, hey; Hey baby, hey child, hey now". It was released in late 1958 on ''[[The Fabulous Little Richard]]'' and in April 1959 as a single.<ref name="White">
{{cite book
| last = White
| first = Charles
| title = The Life and Times of Little Richard: The Quasar of Rock
| year = 1994
| publisher = [[Da Capo Press]]
| isbn = 0-306-80552-9
| page = 259
}}</ref>

On May 9, 1956, Little Richard recorded "[[Hey-Hey-Hey-Hey!|Hey-Hey-Hey-Hey]]", also known as "Hey-Hey-Hey-Hey! (Goin' Back to Birmingham)",<ref name="Ace" /> which was similar to a part of the second version of "Kansas City" recorded six months earlier. Credited to Richard, it was released in January 1958 as the B-side of "[[Good Golly, Miss Molly]]" and in July 1958 on ''[[Little Richard (album)|Little Richard]]''.<ref name="White" />

In 1959, after several years of performing Littlefield's "K. C. Loving", [[Wilbert Harrison]] decided to record the song. In March 1959, after [[Little Richard]]'s version was released, Harrison, with a trio including guitarist [[Wild Jimmy Spruill]], recorded it in a New York studio for producer [[Bobby Robinson (record producer)|Bobby Robinson]] of [[Fury Records]].<ref name="Bronson">{{Cite book
| last = Bronson
| first = Fred
| author-link = Fred Bronson
| title = The Billboard Book of Number 1 Hits
| publisher = Billboard Books
| year = 2003
| isbn = 978-0-8230-7677-2
| page = 53
}}</ref> "Kansas City" was released on a single by Fury later that year.

Although the song's arrangement varied little from Littlefield's, it "struck such a solid shuffle groove that it was unforgettable", with inspired rhythm and solo guitar work by Spruill.<ref name="Marsh">{{Cite book
| last = Marsh
| first = Dave
| author-link = Dave Marsh
| title = The Heart of Rock & Soul: The 1001 Greatest Singles Ever Made
| publisher = [[Da Capo Press]]
| year = 1999
| isbn = 978-0-306-80901-9
| pages = 125–127
}}</ref><ref>{{cite AV media notes
| last = Forte
| first = Dan
| year = 1990
| title = Legends of Guitar — Rock, The 50s Vol. 1
| type = Album notes
| others = Various artists
| publisher = [[Rhino Records]]
| id = R2 70719
| pages = 5–6
}}</ref> Harrison's song was issued with Leiber and Stoller's original name, "Kansas City", but changed the refrain to "They got some crazy little women there, and I'm gonna get me one"<ref name=pc13 /> and dropped one twelve-bar section.

Shortly after the song's release, several other versions appeared. ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine's pop song pick of the week for March 30, 1959, listed five different releases of "Kansas City": Harrison's and versions by [[Hank Ballard]] and [[The Midnighters]],<ref>King 5195</ref> Rocky Olson,<ref>[[Chess Records|Chess]] 1723</ref> Rockin' Ronald & the Rebels,<ref>[[End Records|End]] 1043</ref> and a reissue by Littlefield.<ref>Federal 12351</ref> A week later, the magazine announced the single release of a version by Little Richard. Although Ballard's and Richard's versions both appeared in the lower reaches of the ''Billboard'' charts, Harrison's was a runaway hit, reaching number one in both the R&B and pop charts, where it remained for seven weeks,<ref>{{Cite book
| last = Whitburn
| first = Joel
| author-link = Joel Whitburn
| year = 1988
| section = Wilbert Harrison
| title = Top R&B Singles 1942–1988
| location = Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin
| publisher = [[Record Research]]
| isbn = 0-89820-068-7
| page = [https://archive.org/details/joelwhitburnstop00whit/page/183 183]
| url = https://archive.org/details/joelwhitburnstop00whit/page/183
}}</ref> and became one of the top selling records of 1959.<ref>Whitburn 1988, p. 600.</ref> In Belgium, the single reached numbers 18 in Flanders<ref>{{Cite web
| url = https://www.ultratop.be/nl/song/2b11c/Wilbert-Harrison-Kansas-City
| title = Wilbert Harrison: 'Kansas City'
| website = [[Ultratop]].com
| access-date = May 31, 2021
}}</ref> and 24 in Wallonia.<ref>{{cite web
| url = https://www.ultratop.be/fr/song/2b11c/Wilbert-Harrison-Kansas-City
| title = Wilbert Harrison: 'Kansas City'
| website = [[Ultratop]].com
| access-date = May 31, 2021
}}</ref> Harrison also recorded an [[answer song]] to the same tune as "Kansas City", called "Goodbye Kansas City", which was released on a single by Fury Records in 1960.

In 1959, after several years of performing Littlefield's "K. C. Loving", Wilbert Harrison decided to record the song. In March 1959, after Little Richard's version was released, Harrison, with a trio including guitarist Wild Jimmy Spruill, recorded it in a New York studio for producer Bobby Robinson of Fury Records. "Kansas City" was released on a single by Fury later that year.

Although the song's arrangement varied little from Littlefield's, it "struck such a solid shuffle groove that it was unforgettable", with inspired rhythm and solo guitar work by Spruill. Harrison's song was issued with Leiber and Stoller's original name, "Kansas City", but changed the refrain to "They got some crazy little women there, and I'm gonna get me one" and dropped one twelve-bar section.

Shortly after the song's release, several other versions appeared. Billboard magazine's pop song pick of the week for March 30, 1959, listed five different releases of "Kansas City": Harrison's and versions by Hank Ballard and The Midnighters, Rocky Olson, Rockin' Ronald & the Rebels, and a reissue by Littlefield. A week later, the magazine announced the single release of a version by Little Richard. Although Ballard's and Richard's versions both appeared in the lower reaches of the Billboard charts, Harrison's was a runaway hit, reaching number one in both the R&B and pop charts, where it remained for seven weeks, and became one of the top selling records of 1959. In Belgium, the single reached numbers 18 in Flanders and 24 in Wallonia. Harrison also recorded an answer song to the same tune as "Kansas City", called "Goodbye Kansas City", which was released on a single by Fury Records in 1960.

sections.heading: Background
Recording
sections.wikitext:
On Sunday, October 18, 1964, during a day off from their 1964 UK Tour, the Beatles recorded a medley of "Kansas City"/"Hey, Hey, Hey, Hey".{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=50}} While rehearsing the song, McCartney found some parts difficult to sing. He later recalled that [[John Lennon]] pulled him aside and encouraged him, saying, "Come on man, you can do it better than this, get up there!".{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=11}} Recorded in only two takes, take one was marked "best".{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=50}} Each take includes a different guitar solo from [[George Harrison]], indicating he [[Musical improvisation|improvised]].{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=267}} Harrison plays his [[Gretsch|Country Gent]] guitar and Lennon plays his 1958 [[Rickenbacker]] 325 Capri.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=268}} Producer [[George Martin]] [[overdubbing|overdubbed]] a piano contribution on his [[Steinway & Sons|Steinway]] and [[Ringo Starr]] provided the drums.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=268}} Lewisohn describes the part as "barely discernible on record."{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=50}} Martin and engineers [[Norman Smith (record producer)|Norman Smith]] and Tony Clark mixed the track for mono and stereo on October 26.{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=51}}

The track differs from Little Richard's in its simplified walking bass and triplet piano chords, which MacDonald writes, "[imparts] a sassy swing to a performance let down only by its lightweight mono mix."{{sfn|MacDonald|2005|p=135}} MacDonald concludes that it is "one of the Beatles' best covers."{{sfn|MacDonald|2005|p=136}}

He later recalled that John Lennon pulled him aside and encouraged him, saying, "Come on man, you can do it better than this, get up there!".{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=11}} Recorded in only two takes, take one was marked "best".{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=50}} Each take includes a different guitar solo from George Harrison, indicating he improvised.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=267}} Harrison plays his Country Gent guitar and Lennon plays his 1958 Rickenbacker 325 Capri.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=268}} Producer George Martin overdubbed a piano contribution on his Steinway and Ringo Starr provided the drums.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=268}} Lewisohn describes the part as "barely discernible on record."{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=50}} Martin and engineers Norman Smith and Tony Clark mixed the track for mono and stereo on October 26.{{sfn|Lewisohn|1988|p=51}}

sections.heading: Release
sections.wikitext:
The Beatles released the track in the UK on December 4, 1964, on their album ''[[Beatles for Sale]]''. Release in the US came the following year on June 14, 1965, on ''[[Beatles VI]]''.{{sfn|MacDonald|2005|p=135}} As part of [[Capitol Records]]' "Starline" series, the track was the [[B-side]] of "[[Boys (The Shirelles song)|Boys]]" on an October 1965 single.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=214}}

The Beatles released take two on the 1995 compilation album ''[[Anthology 1]]'',{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=267}} a version MacDonald calls "only slightly less successful".{{sfn|MacDonald|2005|p=135n}} This version does not include Martin's piano overdub.{{sfn|MacDonald|2005|p=135n}} A live version, recorded in Hamburg in December 1962, is included on the 1977 release ''Live! at the Star-Club in Hamburg, Germany; 1962''.{{sfn|Everett|2001|p=138}} Other live versions appear on the albums ''[[Live at the BBC (Beatles album)|Live at the BBC]]'' and ''[[On Air – Live at the BBC Volume 2]]'' and in the film ''[[Let It Be (1970 film)|Let It Be]]''. The Beatles appeared on the American television program ''[[Shindig!]]'' performing the medley live in October 1964.

McCartney released his own recording of "Kansas City" on his 1988 cover album ''[[CHOBA B CCCP]]'', though it was only available in the Soviet Union until 1991.

* [[Ringo Starr]] - drums, claps
* [[George Martin]] - piano

An instrumental version was featured on the 1968 album James Brown Plays Nothing But Soul entitled "Buddy E" and a later, funkier version with many returning musicians appears on the 1975 album Everybody's Doin' the Hustle & Dead on the Double Bump. Brown recorded live performances of the song for his albums Live at the Apollo, Volume II (1968), Say It Live and Loud (1998; recorded 1968) and Live At Home With His Bad Self (2019; recorded 1969), and in his concert films James Brown: Man to Man and Live at the Boston Garden.  This was also James Brown's first single to be reissued by Polydor Records.

At Brown's request, singer Marva Whitney performed "Kansas City" at the conclusion of his public funeral in Augusta, Georgia in 2006.

In 2005, [[Kansas City, Missouri|Kansas City]] adopted "Kansas City" as its official song, dedicating "Goin' to Kansas City Plaza" in the historic [[18th and Vine Historic District|18th and Vine]] Jazz district. Due to redevelopment, the "12th Street and Vine" intersection mentioned in the song no longer exists, but a park roughly in the shape of a grand piano and with a path in the shape of a [[treble clef]] exists at the former location, marked by a commemorative plaque. Some versions have substituted "Eighteenth and Vine" for "12th Street and Vine," which sings just as well, and recognizes Kansas City's jazz history.<ref name="kcs120423">{{cite news |first1=Suzanne P. |last1=Cole |first2=Tim |last2=Engle |first3=Eric |last3=Winkler |work=[[Kansas City Star]] |title=50 things every Kansas Citian should know |url=http://www.kansascity.com/2012/04/19/3564081/50-things-every-kansas-citian.html |date=April 23, 2012 |access-date=April 23, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://maps.google.com/maps?hl=en&q=1550%20E%2012th%20street%20kansas%20city&um=1&ie=UTF-8&sa=N&tab=wl |title=12th Street and Vine, Kansas City |website=[[Google Maps|maps.google.com]] |access-date=January 8, 2011}}</ref>

In 2026, the Royals second City Connect jersey included the phrase "HEY HEY HEY HEY" inside the collar of the jersey as a nod to the song.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Royals unveil new City Connects, with hidden nod to Beatles |url=https://www.mlb.com/news/royals-release-city-connect-2-0-jerseys}}</ref>

In 2001, Harrison's "Kansas City" received a Grammy Hall of Fame Award and it is included on the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's list of the "500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll". At various times, Harrison's and the Beatles versions have been played over the loud speakers at Kauffman Stadium following Kansas City Royals baseball games.

In 2005, Kansas City adopted "Kansas City" as its official song, dedicating "Goin' to Kansas City Plaza" in the historic 18th and Vine Jazz district. Due to redevelopment, the "12th Street and Vine" intersection mentioned in the song no longer exists, but a park roughly in the shape of a grand piano and with a path in the shape of a treble clef exists at the former location, marked by a commemorative plaque. Some versions have substituted "Eighteenth and Vine" for "12th Street and Vine," which sings just as well, and recognizes Kansas City's jazz history.

In 2026, the Royals second City Connect jersey included the phrase "HEY HEY HEY HEY" inside the collar of the jersey as a nod to the song.
